title: Sigma and Pi Bond Formation Visualization
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: AP Chemistry
description: Interactive side-by-side comparison of sigma (end-on) and pi (side-by-side) orbital overlap, each with a side view and a view along the internuclear axis. A twist slider shows that sigma overlap is unchanged by rotation while pi overlap falls to zero at 90 degrees. Cards count the sigma and pi bonds in single, double, and triple bonds.

learningObjectives: Distinguish sigma and pi bonds by their orbital overlap patterns
Explain why pi bonds restrict molecular rotation
Count sigma and pi bonds in single, double, and triple bonds
standards: AP Chemistry CED Unit 2, Topic 2.7: VSEPR and Hybridization

controls.label: Twist angle
controls.description: Rotates atom 2 about the internuclear axis from 0 to 90 degrees; switched off for the triple bond

controls.label: Bond cards
controls.description: Clicking a card selects that bond type

equations: pi overlap is proportional to cos(twist angle)
single = 1 sigma; double = 1 sigma + 1 pi; triple = 1 sigma + 2 pi
assumptions: Orbital lobes are schematic outlines, not calculated electron densities
Orbital phases (signs) are not shown; color identifies the atom
The twist test is shown for the double bond only

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Side-by-side comparison with a predict-then-test parameter slider
keyQuestions: Where is the electron density of a sigma bond? Of a pi bond?
Why can a single bond rotate while a double bond cannot?
How many sigma and pi bonds are in ethene?
commonMisconceptions: A double bond is two identical bonds
A pi bond is two bonds because it has two lobes
Pi bonds can form without a sigma bond
assessmentOpportunities: Students predict the overlap at 90 degrees before moving the slider
Students count sigma and pi bonds in ethane, ethene, and ethyne
